sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Scenario-based questions are how interviewers test whether you have actually written Go, not just read about it. They present you with a snippet of real-looking code and ask 'what does this print?', 'what is the bug?', or 'how would you fix this?'. The seven scenarios in this module — goroutine vs thread, channel direction, interface vs struct, pointer vs value, nil map, defer ordering, and error handling — cover the most frequently tested Go fresher gotchas.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
Five 'surprise' patterns that appear in almost every Go scenario question:

- **The loop-variable goroutine capture** — `go func() { fmt.Println(i) }()` inside a for loop captures the variable `i`, not its current value. By the time the goroutine runs, `i` has advanced. Fix: pass `i` as an argument.
- **The nil map panic on write** — `var m map[string]int; m["k"] = 1` panics. Reading from a nil map returns zero silently. Writing panics.
- **The pointer receiver and interface satisfaction** — a concrete type `T` with only pointer-receiver methods does not satisfy an interface when stored as a value. Only `*T` does.
- **Defer LIFO with immediate argument evaluation** — deferred functions run last-in-first-out. Arguments to deferred calls are evaluated at the `defer` statement, not at function return.
- **Error wrapping and `errors.Is`** — `fmt.Errorf("%w", err)` wraps; `err == ErrNotFound` fails on a wrapped error; `errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound)` unwraps and checks correctly.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **Goroutine vs thread scenario** — goroutines are lightweight (2 KB start stack), scheduled by the Go runtime; OS threads are ~1 MB; the Go runtime multiplexes N goroutines onto M OS threads
- **Channel direction scenario** — `chan<- T` is send-only, `<-chan T` is receive-only; function parameters use directional channels to express intent and prevent misuse
- **Interface vs struct scenario** — accept interfaces, return concrete types (Go design proverb); a function that accepts `io.Writer` instead of `*os.File` can work with files, HTTP responses, and buffers
- **Pointer vs value scenario** — pointer receiver methods mutate the receiver; value receiver methods operate on a copy; storing a `T` value in an interface variable only satisfies the interface if all methods are value-receiver
- **Nil map scenario** — `var m map[K]V` is nil; reading returns zero value (safe); writing panics (must use `make`); checking `m == nil` is the correct nil test
- **Defer ordering scenario** — deferred calls execute in LIFO order; argument values are captured at the defer statement; a named return variable can be modified by a deferred function
- **Error handling scenario** — always check errors; wrap with context using `%w`; use `errors.Is` for sentinel checks; return `nil` error only on genuine success

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **'What does this print?' with loop goroutines** — the classic: `for i := 0; i < 3; i++ { go func() { fmt.Println(i) }() }` — prints `3 3 3` (or some non-deterministic combination of 3s), not `0 1 2`. Every Go interviewer uses this.
- **'Why doesn't this compile?' with interface + value receiver** — storing a `User` value (not `*User`) in a `Stringer` interface when `String()` is a pointer receiver method. The fix: use `&user` instead of `user`.
- **'Spot the bug' with nil map** — `func NewCache() Cache { var c Cache; c.data["key"] = val; return c }` panics because `c.data` is nil. The fix: `c.data = make(map[string]string)`.
- **'What is the output?' with defer + named return** — `func f() (result int) { defer func() { result++ }(); return 1 }` returns `2`, not `1`. The deferred function increments the named return variable after `return 1` sets it.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"When I see a scenario question in a Go interview, I look for five things: loop variable captures in goroutine closures, nil map writes, pointer-vs-value receiver and interface satisfaction, defer argument evaluation timing, and error wrapping that breaks a direct equality check. For the loop capture specifically — if a goroutine closure uses a loop variable, I pass it as an argument to the goroutine function to capture the current value rather than the reference. These are the patterns that show up most often in production bugs as well as in interviews."*
